questions.q: Beyond the catalog itself, what does a Backstage-style developer portal actually add for a developer looking at one service's page?
options: A replacement for the Terraform state file covered earlier in this path
A single view combining ownership, dependencies, docs, pipeline status, and runtime health, instead of pinging several teams separately
A tool that automatically writes a service's business logic for the developer
A static export of the catalog with no live data at all
questions.explain: The portal is the layer on top of the catalog where a developer sees everything about a service -- ownership, dependencies, docs, deploy status, runtime health -- in one page instead of checking several separate systems.

questions.q: What problem does TechDocs' docs-as-code approach solve that a traditional wiki does not?
options: It makes documentation optional for any service tagged production
It encrypts documentation so only the owning team can read it
It keeps docs accurate because they're committed in the same repo and reviewed in the same pull request as the code change that makes them necessary
It replaces the need to write any documentation at all
questions.explain: Because Markdown docs live in the same repository as the code, under the same review process, nothing forces them to drift the way an unenforced, separately maintained wiki page does.

questions.q: What is a Backstage plugin, as described in this lesson?
options: A required field inside every catalog-info.yaml file
A separate login system that replaces the portal's authentication
A one-time migration script run when a service is first created
A self-contained module that renders live data, such as CI/CD status or Kubernetes health, as a tab on an entity's page
questions.explain: Backstage's core is deliberately thin; almost everything a developer actually sees on an entity page -- pipeline status, pod health, cost data -- is contributed by a plugin reading that entity's own metadata.

questions.q: Why can't a Kubernetes plugin show a service's live pod health without the catalog entity underneath it being accurate?
options: The plugin reads the entity's own metadata, such as a namespace annotation, to know what to query -- without accurate metadata it has nothing to fetch against
Kubernetes plugins do not actually require any catalog data to function
Pod health is calculated entirely from the service's TechDocs content
The plugin instead queries a separate spreadsheet maintained by the Kubernetes team
questions.explain: A plugin's whole job is to look at an entity's metadata and know what to query from a live system. If that metadata is missing or wrong, the plugin has nothing reliable to point at.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what fundamentally distinguishes a developer portal from a wiki?
options: A portal requires significantly more manual upkeep than a wiki to stay useful
A wiki and a portal are functionally identical once a catalog exists
A wiki is someone's best-effort description of a system from memory; a portal is a live view of the system itself, kept current by docs-as-code and plugins rather than manual upkeep
A portal only works for services written in one specific programming language
questions.explain: The portal surfaces the catalog's real data through TechDocs and plugins that pull live information, which is what keeps it current without the manual maintenance a wiki depends on and usually doesn't get.
